title: Over 25% of people lie to get antibiotics—and their lies aren't even good
gist: Two linked JAMA Network Open studies led by Alistair Thorpe at the University of Utah found that 28% of 959 valid adult survey respondents (and 27% of caregivers) admitted misrepresenting symptoms to get antibiotics. The lies were mostly cold-like symptoms that don't call for antibiotics, yet 77% of adults and 87% of caregivers said they got the prescription. A commentary by Northwestern's Jeffrey Linder argues the bigger harm is eroded clinician-patient trust.

themes.theme: Prevalence and type of patient deception

insights.claim: Of 959 valid and complete survey responses, 268 (28%) said they had misrepresented symptoms to get antibiotics: 108 exaggerated, 19 fabricated and 141 did both. Separately, 63 of 263 caregivers (27%) said they had misrepresented a child's symptoms.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: More than a quarter of patients game prescribing decisions, which undercuts the reliability of symptom-based diagnosis.

insights.claim: Cold-related symptoms were the most common lie, reported by 65% of dishonest patients. Next came stomach symptoms (49%), joint or muscle pain (46%), general malaise (37%), eye symptoms (34%), skin conditions (32.5%) and urinary symptoms (31%).
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Most of the lies target viral-type complaints that antibiotics cannot treat.

insights.claim: The most common reasons for lying were feeling the illness was particularly severe, believing antibiotics were the only thing that would help, wanting to get back to work or school faster, and wanting personal autonomy over treatment.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Patient demand comes from perceived severity and time pressure, not just ignorance.

insights.claim: Patients who lied tended to be younger and to feel clinicians didn't take their symptoms seriously. They were more likely to believe antibiotic resistance is a hoax, to have more underlying conditions, to see lying as more acceptable and to need help reading health materials. Non-liars had more antibiotic knowledge.

insights.claim: For any single patient, resistance is probably irrelevant. insights.claim: Linder argues that prescribing antibiotics for diagnoses that don't warrant them is medically incorrect and is itself a form of dishonesty meant to placate the patient. Drawing on Sissela Bok, he says such practices lacking in candor threaten the institution of medicine.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: The deeper risk is a loss of trust on both sides, not only resistance.

insights.claim: The study authors call for better communication strategies about antibiotics to address patient concerns, improve understanding of appropriate use and strengthen patient-clinician relationships.
